subject: Accounting
title: Operating Cash Flow
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Operating Cash Flow.

hook.text: Operating cash flow answers a simple question: does the core business generate real money?

buildup.text: It tracks cash from day-to-day operations—sales collected, suppliers paid, wages disbursed.

discovery.text: Positive operating cash flow means the business funds itself. Negative means it's burning reserves.

twist.text: A company can have positive operating cash flow but negative net income—or vice versa.

climax.text: Consistent positive operating cash flow is the strongest sign of a healthy business model.

punchline.text: If operations don't generate cash, nothing else matters.

quiz.question: What does operating cash flow measure?
options: Cash generated from core business activities

details.summary: Operating cash flow measures the cash generated by a company's core business operations—excluding investments and financing. This topic explains the indirect method of calculating OCF, why it differs from net income, and what it reveals about business quality.
details.whyItMatters: Operating cash flow shows whether the core business actually generates cash. A company with growing profits but declining operating cash flow may be heading for trouble.
takeaways: OCF starts with net income and adjusts for non-cash items and changes in working capital
Consistently positive OCF means the core business is self-sustaining without external funding
A growing gap between net income and OCF is a classic warning sign of accounting manipulation

faq.question: How is operating cash flow calculated?
faq.answer: Using the indirect method, start with net income, add back non-cash expenses like depreciation, and adjust for changes in working capital items like receivables, inventory, and payables. The result shows how much cash the core business operations actually generated.

faq.question: Why does operating cash flow differ from net income?
faq.answer: Net income includes non-cash items like depreciation and uses accrual accounting for revenue and expenses. OCF adjusts for these, showing actual cash collected and paid. Rising receivables reduce OCF because revenue was recorded but cash wasn't collected.
